Requirement: As the TLF of associative memory, realize the function of forming links between two previously unrelated stimuli (object, space, context) and recalling the other stimulus when one is presented later. Input: object/context information from [U.LEC-L2] ([LEC-L2] object feature representation and contextual information), spatial information from [U.MEC-L2] ([MEC-L2] spatial location and movement information), contextual information from [U.LEC-L3] ([LEC-L3] contextual information), spatial and temporal control signals from [U.MEC-L3] ([MEC-L3] spatial information and temporal control signals). Output: feedback to [U.EC-L5] and [U.EC-L2/3] ([EC-L5] object memory encoding, [EC-L2/3] memory recall support).
Requirement realization by interface: Interface receives object/space/context information from entorhinal cortex (EC) Layer 2 and Layer 3 as input, and provides feedback of formed associative memories to EC Layer 5 and Layer 2/3 as output. This matches the function defined in Requirement: link formation and recall between stimuli. Hippocampal inputs ([U.LEC-L2], [U.MEC-L2], [U.LEC-L3], [U.MEC-L3]) undergo interference prevention, association formation, and memory stabilization before being fed back to cortex as hippocampal outputs ([U.EC-L5], [U.EC-L2/3]).
Capability: Heteroassociative memory and episodic binding: Computational function to spatiotemporally bind different types of information (object, space, context) and recall complete memories from partial cues. Based on Marr's (1971) hippocampal theory, McNaughton & Morris's (1987) attractor network theory, and Chandra-Sharma et al.'s (2025) Vector-HaSH model. Associative memory is the foundation for the brain to learn relationships between different elements in the environment and form episodic memories.
Mechanism: The hippocampus prevents interference of similar stimuli through pattern separation (DG), forms associations between stimuli through Hebbian learning (CA3), recalls memories from partial cues through pattern completion (CA3), and transforms temporary memories into long-term memories through synaptic stabilization (CA1). These computational steps are executed hierarchically to realize associative memory. Bidirectional information flow where input from EC passes through DG→CA3→CA1 and feeds back to EC integrates memory encoding, consolidation, and retrieval.

Requirement: In associative memory formation, transform input patterns into distinguishable representations to prevent interference between similar stimuli. Input: object/context information from [U.LEC-L2] ([LEC-L2] object feature representation and contextual information) and spatial information from [U.MEC-L2] ([MEC-L2] spatial location and movement information). Output: pattern-separated stimulus representations to [U.CA3-Pyr] and [U.CA3-IN] ([DG] pattern-separated stimulus representation). DG transforms similar input patterns into different output patterns with minimal overlap.
Requirement realization by interface: Interface receives object/context/spatial information from [U.LEC-L2] and [U.MEC-L2] as input, and sends pattern-separated representations to [U.CA3-Pyr] and [U.CA3-IN] as output. This matches the function defined in Requirement: transformation of similar stimuli into distinguishable representations. [U.DG] is the core.
Capability: Pattern separation: Computational transformation of high-dimensional similar inputs into low-overlap outputs. Based on O'Reilly & McClelland's (1994) computational theory. Pattern separation is closely related to competitive learning and sparse coding. Experiments by Leutgeb et al. (2007) confirmed that DG generates representations with minimal overlap. In computational neuroscience, defined as transformation to sparse distributed representations (Marr, 1971).
Mechanism: DG achieves sparse firing where only 2-5% of granule cells are active overall through high firing threshold of granule cells, strong feedforward inhibition, nonlinear integration in dendrites, and feedback inhibition from mossy cells (Myers & Scharfman, 2011). This low activity rate reduces overlap between similar inputs. Heterogeneity of adult-born neurons and semilunar granule cells (SGCs) contributes to dynamic sparsity control (2024 research). Pattern-separated representations are transmitted to CA3 via mossy fibers.

Requirement: Through CA3 recurrent circuits, realize associative memory formation (encoding) and retrieval. Input: object information from [U.LEC-L2] ([LEC-L2] object feature representation), spatial information from [U.MEC-L2] ([MEC-L2] spatial location and movement information), pattern-separated representation from [U.DG] ([DG] pattern-separated stimulus representation), recurrent input from [U.CA3-Pyr] itself ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs), inhibitory signals from [U.CA3-IN] ([CA3-IN] engram-specific inhibitory signals). Output: associative stimulus representation of [U.CA3-Pyr] ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs) transmitted to [U.CA1-Pyr], [U.CA1-PV], [U.CA1-SST].
Requirement realization by interface: Interface integrates information from multiple input sources (direct EC input, mossy fibers from DG, self-recurrent, inhibitory input) and outputs to CA3-Pyr itself, CA3-IN, and neurons in CA1 region. This realizes the function described in Requirement: association formation and retrieval. Particularly, recurrent connections ([U.CA3-Pyr] → [U.CA3-Pyr]) are the foundation for both encoding and pattern completion.
Capability: Heteroassociative memory with attractor dynamics: Computational function to learn associations between different input patterns and recall complete patterns from partial cues. Based on Marr's (1971) and McNaughton & Morris's (1987) CA3 theory. CA3 recurrent connections function as Hopfield-type attractor networks, storing memory patterns as attractor states (Rolls, 2013). Sanchez-Aguilera et al. (2025) showed that heterosynaptic plasticity stabilizes engram formation through selective inhibition.
Mechanism: CA3 recurrent circuit forms associations through Hebbian learning ([R.Hebbian-Linking]) and realizes retrieval through pattern completion ([R.Pattern-Completion]). During encoding, NMDA receptor-dependent LTP is induced between CA3-Pyr neuron populations activated by simultaneously presented stimuli. During retrieval, partial cues activate part of CA3-Pyr, and complete patterns are reconstructed through recurrent connections. Selective inhibition from CA3-IN suppresses competing engrams and improves retrieval precision. Strong input from mossy fibers promotes formation of novel patterns (detonator effect).

Requirement: In CA1, integrate and stabilize associative memories formed in CA3, and provide feedback to cortex. Input: Schaffer collaterals from [U.CA3-Pyr] ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs), temporoammonic input from [U.MEC-L3] and [U.LEC-L3] ([MEC-L3] spatial information and temporal control signals, [LEC-L3] contextual information), inhibitory signals from [U.CA1-PV] and [U.CA1-SST] ([CA1-PV] perisomatic inhibitory signals, [CA1-SST] distal dendritic inhibitory signals). Output: feedback to [U.EC-L5] and [U.EC-L2/3] ([EC-L5] object memory encoding, [EC-L2/3] memory recall support).
Requirement realization by interface: Interface integrates main input from CA3 and direct input from EC, generates output to EC under precise control by inhibitory interneurons. This matches the function defined in Requirement: memory integration, stabilization, and feedback. Integration of both CA3 and EC Layer 3 inputs is the foundation of heterosynaptic plasticity (Pena et al., 2026).
Capability: Memory integration and systems consolidation: Computational function to transform temporary associative memories formed in hippocampal CA3 into long-term stable representations and provide feedback to cortex. Based on systems consolidation theory (Squire & Alvarez, 1995) and CA1 information integration model (Hasselmo, 2005). Wang et al. (2025) showed that progressive stabilization of CA1 place cells contributes to memory formation. CA1 replays memories during SWR (sharp wave-ripple) events from CA3 and propagates them to cortex, promoting memory consolidation (Buzsaki, 2015).
Mechanism: CA1 integrates inputs from two pathways: CA3 and EC Layer 3 ([R.Memory-Integration]). Early in learning, CA3 input dominates, and BTSP (Behavioral Timescale Synaptic Plasticity) is induced within CA1, stabilizing place cells (Wang et al., 2025). Plastic inhibition (iLTD/iLTP) by CA1-PV and CA1-SST adjusts the balance between CA3 and EC inputs, promoting memory consolidation (Udakis et al., 2020). Stabilized memories are transmitted to cortex through feedback pathways from CA1 to EC ([R.Memory-Output]). Hierarchical temporal structure of theta and gamma oscillations controls timing of encoding and retrieval.

Requirement: Through Hebbian synaptic plasticity, strengthen synaptic connections between neural populations that are co-activated in temporal proximity to form associations. Input: object information from [U.LEC-L2] ([LEC-L2] object feature representation), spatial information from [U.MEC-L2] ([MEC-L2] spatial location and movement information), pattern-separated representation from [U.DG] ([DG] pattern-separated stimulus representation), recurrent input from [U.CA3-Pyr] itself ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs), inhibitory signals from [U.CA3-IN] ([CA3-IN] engram-specific inhibitory signals). Output: strengthened synaptic connections of [U.CA3-Pyr] ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs).
Requirement realization by interface: Interface receives multiple excitatory inputs (EC, DG, CA3 recurrent) and inhibitory input (CA3-IN), outputs to CA3-Pyr itself and CA3-IN. This matches the function defined in Requirement: strengthening connections between co-activated populations. [U.CA3-Pyr] implements Hebbian plasticity through recurrent connections, [U.CA3-IN] provides selective inhibition.
Capability: Hebbian associative learning: Computational principle to strengthen synaptic connections between co-activated neurons. Based on Hebb's (1949) cells that fire together, wire together. This principle is implemented by NMDA receptor-dependent LTP (Bliss & Lømo, 1973). Hebbian learning is the foundation of unsupervised learning and the basic mechanism by which the brain learns statistical structure of the environment. CA3 recurrent circuit is an ideal structure for implementing Hebbian learning (McNaughton & Morris, 1987).
Mechanism: During encoding, NMDA receptor-dependent LTP is induced between CA3-Pyr neuron populations activated by simultaneously presented stimuli A and B. Recurrent connection weight matrix W is updated according to Hebbian rule (ΔW ∝ [U.CA3-Pyr]_pre × [U.CA3-Pyr]_post). Temporal contiguity is also included in Hebbian learning, with co-activation within time window strengthening connections. Heterosynaptic plasticity from CA3-IN learns engram-specific inhibitory patterns, improving precision of Hebbian learning (Sanchez-Aguilera et al., 2025). Strong input from mossy fibers exceeds CA3-Pyr threshold, initiating formation of novel patterns (detonator effect).

Requirement: Through recurrent circuits, reconstruct complete patterns from partial cues and recall associative memories. Input: mossy fibers from [U.DG] ([DG] pattern-separated stimulus representation, partial cues), recurrent input from [U.CA3-Pyr] ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs), inhibitory signals from [U.CA3-IN] ([CA3-IN] engram-specific inhibitory signals). Output: complete pattern of [U.CA3-Pyr] ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs).
Requirement realization by interface: Interface receives partial cues ([U.DG]), recurrent input ([U.CA3-Pyr]), and inhibitory input ([U.CA3-IN]), outputs complete pattern. This matches the function defined in Requirement: complete pattern reconstruction from partial cues. [U.CA3-Pyr] recurrent circuit executes pattern completion, [U.CA3-IN] suppresses competing engrams.
Capability: Pattern completion in attractor networks: Computational principle where partial initial states converge to complete attractor states in attractor networks. Based on Hopfield's (1982) attractor neural network and Marr's (1971) hippocampal theory. Pattern completion is the computational foundation of the brain's ability to recall memories from noisy partial cues. Rolls (2013) showed that CA3 recurrent connections are structures optimized for pattern completion.
Mechanism: During retrieval, partial cues (part of stimulus A) activate part of CA3-Pyr. Through recurrent connections, activity propagates to neuron populations corresponding to stimulus B. This propagation process is described as convergence to an attractor. Selective inhibition from CA3-IN suppresses competing engrams, stabilizing convergence to correct attractor state (Sanchez-Aguilera et al., 2025). If recurrent connection strength is sufficient, complete patterns are reconstructed from partial activation. Success of pattern completion depends on strength of synaptic connections formed during Hebbian learning.

Requirement: Integrate associative memories from CA3 and direct input from EC to stabilize memory representations. Input: Schaffer collaterals from [U.CA3-Pyr] ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs), temporoammonic input from [U.MEC-L3] and [U.LEC-L3] ([MEC-L3] spatial information and temporal control signals, [LEC-L3] contextual information), distal dendritic inhibition from [U.CA1-SST] ([CA1-SST] distal dendritic inhibitory signals). Output: stabilized memory representation of [U.CA1-Pyr] ([CA1-Pyr] stabilized associative memory representation) fed back to [U.EC-L5] and [U.EC-L2/3].
Requirement realization by interface: Interface receives input from both CA3 and EC Layer 3, generates stabilized representation under control of dendritic inhibition by CA1-SST. This matches the function defined in Requirement: memory integration and stabilization. [U.CA1-Pyr] stabilizes through BTSP, [U.CA1-SST] adjusts balance between CA3 and EC inputs (iLTP).
Capability: Memory integration and BTSP-based stabilization: Computational function to integrate inputs from multiple sources and stabilize memories through behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP). Based on Wang et al.'s (2025) CA1 place cell stabilization study and Udakis et al.'s (2020) CA1 interneuron plasticity study. BTSP acts on longer timescales (seconds to minutes) than traditional LTP/LTD, supporting memory formation during behavior.
Mechanism: CA1-Pyr integrates inputs from two pathways: CA3 and EC Layer 3. Early in learning, CA3 input dominates, and associative patterns formed in CA3 are transmitted to CA1. BTSP is induced within CA1, stabilizing place cells (Wang et al., 2025). Distal dendritic inhibition (iLTP) by CA1-SST adjusts influence of temporoammonic input from EC, and as learning progresses, CA1 shifts from CA3-dependent to EC-dependent (Udakis et al., 2020). CA1-SST inhibition controls dendritic spikes and calcium signaling, promoting location-specific synaptic plasticity. Stabilized memory representations are fed back to EC.

Requirement: Provide feedback of stabilized memories to cortex to realize memory consolidation and transfer. Input: Schaffer collaterals from [U.CA3-Pyr] ([CA3-Pyr] representation of associated stimulus pairs), perisomatic inhibition from [U.CA1-PV] ([CA1-PV] perisomatic inhibitory signals). Output: feedback from [U.CA1-Pyr] to [U.EC-L5] and [U.EC-L2/3] ([EC-L5] object memory encoding, [EC-L2/3] memory recall support).
Requirement realization by interface: Interface receives input from CA3 and perisomatic inhibition from CA1-PV, generates output to EC. This matches the function defined in Requirement: feedback of memories to cortex. [U.CA1-Pyr] carries projections to EC, [U.CA1-PV] controls timing of output by regulating theta oscillations.
Capability: Hippocampal-cortical feedback and systems consolidation: Computational function to provide feedback of memories processed in hippocampus to cortex and consolidate as long-term memories. Based on systems consolidation theory (Squire & Alvarez, 1995) and Igarashi et al.'s (2025) CA1-EC feedback study. Feedback occurs through two parallel pathways (Layer 5 and Layer 2/3), each serving different functions (encoding and retrieval).
Mechanism: CA1-Pyr projects to EC through two parallel feedback pathways. Disynaptic pathway (CA1→Subiculum→EC Layer 5) mediates object memory encoding, inducing homosynaptic potentiation. Monosynaptic pathway (CA1→EC Layer 2/3) supports memory recall, generating heterosynaptic plasticity and feedforward inhibition (Igarashi et al., 2025). CA1-PV functions as pacemaker of theta oscillations, controlling timing of feedback by restricting CA1-Pyr firing time window. iLTD activity-dependently adjusts CA1-PV→CA1-Pyr connections, supporting place cell stabilization and environmental representation switching (Udakis et al., 2020). Memory replay during sharp wave-ripple (SWR) propagates through feedback pathways to cortex, promoting memory consolidation (Buzsaki, 2015).
